trials.fixtures: fixtures/01-whisper: 3 synthetic English product-explainer narrations (keyboard.wav 38.9 s / 6 cues, thermos.wav 30.2 s / 5 cues, kettle.wav 30.3 s / 5 cues; espeak-ng en-us -s 150, per-sentence synthesis, silence-trimmed, 16 kHz mono s16, 0.4 s gaps so cue times are exact; 3.2 MB total). Per file: <name>.clean.srt (control, correct) and <name>.seeded.srt. KEY.json: 8 defects = 5 text (D1 45->54, D3 dropped 'smooth', D4 'Polar'->'Arctic' Flask, D6 added 'under', D7 temperature->pressure) + 3 timing (D2 start +450 ms, D5 cue -600 ms, D8 cue +900 ms). check_srt.py (faster-whisper word_timestamps -> difflib alignment of normalised tokens to cues -> per-cue WER, missing number/name tokens, start/end error ms), score.py (recall vs KEY, FPs on controls, runtime), make-fixtures.sh + gen_fixtures.py + make-fixtures.log (every command).

baseline.what: no ASR check (subtitles are timed from the script and the voice pipeline; nothing compares audio to cues)

logic_selftest.what: NOT an ASR measurement. score.py --mock feeds check_srt.py synthetic word timings derived from the clean SRTs (words spread evenly over each true cue) to verify the alignment, WER, number/name and timing logic end to end.
logic_selftest.note: With the first-draft threshold 0.05 < WER <= 0.08 the three single-word defects (1 word in 13-15 = WER 0.067-0.077) were missed, so the default threshold is 0.05. Real ASR errors on the TTS voice will therefore also land above the threshold; that is what the blocked run would have measured.

candidate_default.config: base.en, int8 on CPU, beam_size 1, word_timestamps=True, no VAD, WER threshold 0.05 per cue, timing limit 300 ms (end +200 ms slack), numbers normalised to digits, number/name tokens must be heard
candidate_default.error: httpx2.ProxyError: 403 Forbidden (huggingface_hub.snapshot_download of Systran/faster-whisper-base.en; agent proxy: 'gateway answered 403 to CONNECT (policy denial or upstream failure)', host huggingface.co:443; fails after 0.9 s on all 6 wav/srt pairs). Full traceback: runs/01-whisper/model-download.err; per-pair JSON: runs/01-whisper/default.*.json

candidate_tuned.config: small.en, int8 on CPU, beam_size 5, vad_filter=True (Silero VAD via onnxruntime), same thresholds
candidate_tuned.error: same as default: httpx2.ProxyError: 403 Forbidden for huggingface.co (Systran/faster-whisper-small.en); runs/01-whisper/tuned.*.json

limits: Model weights must come from huggingface.co on first run (or be copied into a folder and passed via --model-dir / WHISPER_MODEL_DIR); the sandbox denies that host, so no ASR ran here.

The checker is English-only as configured (base.en / small.en); the real task is 10 languages, which needs the multilingual 'base' / 'small' / 'medium' models (same API, --language xx), larger downloads and generally worse word timestamps for non-English.

Single-word defects force a per-cue WER threshold of 0.05 (one word in a <= 20-word cue); any ASR misrecognition of the TTS voice at that level is a false positive. The number/name rule is independent of the threshold and is the robust part.
Word end timestamps in Whisper are less precise than starts; the end check gets +200 ms slack. A start-only shift is still caught by the start check.

Fixture audio is espeak-ng (robotic). Real pipeline voices (neural TTS / human) usually transcribe better, so the sandbox numbers, once obtained, are a pessimistic bound for text and a fair test for timing.
CPU int8 runtime per 30-40 s clip was not measured; expect seconds for base.en and tens of seconds for small.en on a laptop CPU, plus a one-off model load.
trials.verdict: NOT RUN (blocked: huggingface.co denied by network policy)
trials.reason: Install, fixtures, checker, scorer and wrapper are complete and the detection logic passes an 8/8, 0-FP self-test on synthetic word timings, but the Whisper weights could not be fetched (proxy 403 to CONNECT huggingface.co:443), so recall/false positives/runtime of the real ASR are unmeasured. Owner can finish the trial locally with: bash runs/01-whisper/commands.sh (needs internet once, or a pre-downloaded model folder).

install.command: npm i gltf-validator@2.0.0-dev.3.10 @gltf-transform/cli@4.5.1 (pre-installed: 16.1 s, 68 MB); trial extras: npm i three@0.186.1 pngjs@7.0.0 pixelmatch@8.0.0 (1.6 s, +41 MB, only needed for the render/diff harness, not for the check)

The render harness needs Playwright's Chromium download (blocked here from CDNs, pre-provisioned in this sandbox).

found_how.C4: loads, renders, bbox reported finite (three uses accessor min/max), cube visibly broken (4.2% px differ)

baseline.runtime_note: 4.8 s for 7 files including browser launch; 0.25-0.7 s per file

candidate_default.config: gltf-validator validateBytes() with library defaults (maxIssues 100, no overrides); a defect counts as found if the expected code from KEY.json appears at severity 0 (error)
commands: node runs/04-gltf/validate.mjs default validator-default.json fixtures/04-gltf/clean/*.glb fixtures/04-gltf/seeded/*.glb
candidate_default.clean_control_findings: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 infos, 0 hints on both controls
candidate_default.runtime_note: 47.5 ms for all 7 files in one Node process (first call 26 ms warm-up, then ~3 ms per file)

candidate_tuned.config: validateBytes() with maxIssues: 0 (unlimited) and severityOverrides promoting ACCESSOR_INDEX_TRIANGLE_DEGENERATE, UNUSED_OBJECT, ACCESSOR_NON_UNIT, NODE_EMPTY to errors
commands: node runs/04-gltf/validate.mjs tuned validator-tuned.json fixtures/04-gltf/clean/*.glb fixtures/04-gltf/seeded/*.glb
candidate_tuned.note: No measurable gain over default on this set: the only change is UNUSED_OBJECT on C2 becoming a second error. The defaults already report every seeded defect as an error, so the tuned profile is not needed.

transform.default_pipeline: gltf-transform optimize in out (meshopt compression, quantize, weld, simplify, prune, texture-compress auto)
transform.tuned_pipeline: gltf-transform optimize in out --compress quantize --texture-compress webp --simplify false
transform.why_default_grows: BIN shrinks (648 -> 208 B on Box) but the EXT_meshopt_compression JSON metadata adds ~700 B, and texture-compress 'auto' re-encodes the 3750 B PNG via sharp into a 6572 B PNG. On KB-sized assets the fixed overhead dominates. Tuned: quantization alone -8% on Box; webp texture 3750 -> 3124 B gives -12% on BoxTextured.
transform.parity: 256x256 renders from the same fixed camera, pixelmatch threshold 0.1: 0 differing pixels for all four optimised files (the same diff reports 4.2% for the C3/C4 corruptions, so it is sensitive). Default output needs MeshoptDecoder wired into GLTFLoader; tuned output (KHR_mesh_quantization + EXT_texture_webp) loads in stock three.js.
transform.optimised_outputs_validate: all four pass gltf-validator with 0 errors (default outputs get 2 infos: UNSUPPORTED_EXTENSION for EXT_meshopt_compression, UNUSED_OBJECT buffer)

limits: The npm gltf-validator package is a library only (validateBytes); there is no CLI binary in it, so a ~20-line Node wrapper (wrapper-sketch.mjs) or `gltf-transform validate` is needed. The wrapper only resolves external .bin/images relative to the .gltf file.

Fixtures are tiny (1.6 KB and 6 KB) Khronos samples, so the optimisation numbers are not representative of real figure assets: default optimize made both files larger; gains on larger meshes/textures are unmeasured here.
No CC0 sample exists in the Khronos core set; CC-BY-4.0 Cesium assets were used and attribution is kept in the fixtures. Duck (SCEA licence) was discarded.
Pixel parity was checked at 256x256 from one camera with SwiftShader; it cannot see differences hidden by that view or below pixelmatch's 0.1 threshold.
Seeded defects are all structural/data errors the validator is designed for; semantic problems (wrong scale, missing animation, bad materials) are not covered by either tool.
Baseline render harness needs a Chromium download at install time (~460 MB), which CDN blocking prevented here; it was pre-provisioned. The validator itself needs no browser.
gltf-validator version is a dev pre-release (2.0.0-dev.3.10, the only line published to npm).
trials.reason: Validation: baseline catches 2/5 (only defects that throw in GLTFLoader); gltf-validator catches 5/5 by specific error code with 0 findings on both clean controls, in under 50 ms for 7 files, as a 308 KB pure-JS dependency that runs on Windows. Clear measured gain at negligible cost. Optimisation (gltf-transform): default `optimize` made both sample files larger (+16%, +54%) and adds a meshopt decoder requirement; the tuned quantize+webp pipeline gave -8%/-12% with 0 pixel difference, but on KB-sized samples this is unproven for real assets, so keep it as a per-asset, opt-in step until measured on an actual figure model.

trials.parity_method: Each SVG inlined in an HTML page, CSS width 512px (height from viewBox), headless Chromium screenshot, pixelmatch threshold 0.1. Animated spinner: SMIL paused + setCurrentTime and Web Animations paused + currentTime, compared at t=0 and t=400 ms. Harness controls: original t=0 vs t=400 ms differ by 20.08 % (seek works); a recoloured/shifted icon-play differs from the original by 51.07 % (diff detects change).

wrapper.tested: tuned config: exit 0, 10/10 ok, output byte-identical to the CLI run; plain preset-default: exit 1, 5 files / 11 problems (same files the KEY check flags)

limits: Fixtures are synthetic (10 files, 9.4 KB total): written like the site's own icons, but not the site's real files; absolute savings on real logos will differ.

Pixel parity measured in Chromium only (one engine, one size, one font set); Firefox/Safari and /CSS-background embedding not tested. 0 % diff at threshold 0.1 is strict but not proof of identical rendering everywhere.
Animation parity is two frames (t=0, t=400 ms) with paused/seeked SMIL + CSS animations, not a full timeline comparison.
The tuned config gives up 5 points of raw saving (39.2 % vs 44.2 %) to keep ids, <style> and role/aria. Per-file savings 11-74 %; smallest on the a11y logo and the gradient.

svgo 4 preset-default no longer touches viewBox or <title>, but still drops role=img, renames/removes ids and inlines <style>; every default-config breakage is a configuration matter, not a bug. svgo cleanupIds does not treat aria-labelledby as an id reference.
Structural checks use the sax parser (an svgo dependency), not a full SVG DOM; the wrapper sketch uses regexes and assumes well-formed SVG with double-quoted attributes.
The wrapper sketch was run from a directory where `svgo` resolves (scratchpad); in the site repo it needs svgo in devDependencies.

trials.reason: Tuned config: -39.2 % bytes (-31.3 % gzipped) across 10 files, 0 of 58 seeded requirements broken, 0.000 % pixel diff on every file and both animation frames, 0.47 s for 10 files, pure-JS MIT tool that runs on Windows. svgo defaults are NOT safe for this site: 12 breakages in 4 files including a real accessibility break on the logo. Adopt only with the tuned config plus the post-check wrapper, which turned the default-config breakages into exit 1 in testing.

KEY.json = ground-truth cut times (s + frames; crossfades start/mid/end). score.py = scorer (hard cut: |det-t|<=0.25 s; crossfade: within [start-0.25,end+0.25], error vs midpoint). Note: brief said '8 shots, 6 hard + 2 soft' - 8 cuts need 9 shots, so 9 were used. ffmpeg 'gradients' source was tried for one shot but is not deterministic even with seed=, so it was replaced.

threshold.config: detect-threshold (fade-to-black detector; 0/8 as expected, crossfades do not pass through black)

notes: All hard cuts are frame-exact (0 ms error) for baseline and every scenedetect variant; the mean/max timing errors above come only from crossfades, scored against the fade midpoint (detections land at the fade end, 14.0 s, or mid-fade, 23.333 s).

Crossfade 7 (purple overlay -> teal, 23.0-23.5 s) is detected by detect-content/adaptive via a single-frame delta_hue spike of 154 at 23.333 s (hue wrap-around on near-grey blended pixels; see runs/07-scenedetect/stats-seeded.csv). That is an artefact, not genuine fade detection; detect-hist detects both fades without it (13.867 s, 23.033 s).

Crossfade 4 (mandelbrot -> smptebars) has content_val ~5-11 during the fade and 21 at the last fade frame; the default threshold 27 misses it, 15 catches it, detect-adaptive catches it via the ratio to neighbouring frames.
The 'threshold 15' tuning was picked after looking at the stats file, so it is tuned on the answer key; detect-adaptive (pure defaults) is reported as the tuned candidate for that reason.
scenedetect CSV 'Start Frame' is 1-based; the scorer uses 'Start Time (seconds)'. Control clip is 299 frames (overlay shortest=1 drops one), harmless.
limits: Synthetic fixture only (flat colours, test patterns, panning overlays). Real explainer footage with fast camera moves, flashes or animated text was not tested, so the 0-false-positive result is a lower bound of risk, not proof.

Soft transitions: PySceneDetect has no dedicated crossfade/dissolve detector (detect-threshold is fade-to-black only). 0.5 s crossfades were found only by lowered thresholds / adaptive ratio, and one of the two via a hue-wrap artefact.

Install footprint 354 MB (both opencv wheels) - ~230 MB with headless only; adds a Python 3 runtime requirement to a Node project. scenedetect 0.7.2 hard-depends on opencv-python, so a headless CI box should use scenedetect-headless instead (exists on PyPI, not verified here).
Runtime ~3.6 s per 30 s 1080x1920 clip on 4 vCPU (~8x realtime, decode-bound); scales linearly with film length. -d/--downscale and -fs/--frame-skip exist but were not needed.

Default detect-content misses a 0.5 s crossfade (7/8); the check must run detect-adaptive (or -t 15) and the script-beat tolerance must accept 'anywhere inside the fade window', as the wrapper sketch does.
Minimum scene length default 0.6 s: two true cuts closer than that would be merged; explainer films rarely cut faster, but the limit exists.
trials.reason: With detect-adaptive (pure defaults, no per-clip threshold) scenedetect found 8/8 cuts incl. both 0.5 s crossfades with 0 false positives on the seeded clip and on the 10 s motion-only control, frame-exact on hard cuts, in 3.6 s; the 10-minute home-made detector tops out at 5/8 (6/8 with a lower threshold) and structurally cannot see crossfades. Cost is low (BSD-3, pip-only, prebuilt wheels incl. Windows, ~230-354 MB). Caveat: validate false-positive rate on 2-3 real films before trusting it as a gate; one crossfade was caught via a hue-wrap artefact rather than true fade detection.

trials.fixtures: fixtures/08-lighthouse (KEY.json): 'fast' (1.8 KB sized hero, deferred JS) and 'slow' (3.0 MB unsized noise PNG hero, render-blocking 900 ms busy-wait script, banners inserted above content after 1.2 s), served with python3 -m http.server on 127.0.0.1:8765

baseline.what: live HTTP check only: status + total time via curl
baseline.result: fast: 200 in 5 ms; slow: 200 in 1 ms -> the baseline ranks the slow page as the faster one (HTML only, no assets, no rendering)

candidate_default.ranks_correctly: 3/3 runs on score, LCP and CLS; TBT does not separate them

candidate_tuned.finding: Lighthouse 13 no longer ships the performance-budget / timing-budget audits (the JSON has no 'budget' audit): --budget-path is accepted but produces nothing. Budgets must be enforced by our wrapper on the metric values.

limits: Budget audits are gone in Lighthouse 12+: enforce thresholds in the wrapper (checks/perf-budget.mjs does this).
The 900 ms blocking script shows up in FCP/LCP (both 4.4 s on slow), not in TBT, because it runs before first paint; TBT only counts long tasks after FCP.
~11-13 s per run and 187 MB install; run 3 times and take the median for anything near a threshold.
Lab numbers under simulated throttling; they rank pages, they are not field numbers.
trials.reason: Stable ranking (3/3 runs, score sd < 1, LCP sd < 30 ms) where the HTTP baseline ranks the pages the wrong way round; 0 configuration beyond CHROME_PATH. Cost: 187 MB and ~12 s per page.

trials.fixtures: fixtures/09-gitleaks (KEY.json): 10 FAKE secrets K1..K10 in .env, config.json, REPORT.md, notify.js, deploy.log, a .pem; 10 clean files with look-alikes (sha256/sha1 hashes, UUIDs, base64 blob, integrity hash, a Stripe publishable key). The seeded files are NOT stored in git (GitHub push protection rejects even fake tokens): run `node fixtures/09-gitleaks/make-seeded.mjs` first; it writes them from ROT13-encoded text.

baseline.what: none (our key-lint checks test answer keys, not credentials)
baseline.note: A naive keyword grep (password|secret|api_key|token) flags 4 of the 6 seeded files and 1 clean file; it finds files, not secrets.

candidate_default.extra_detail: the Stripe publishable key pk_test_... in seeded/config.json is reported as generic-api-key (publishable keys are public by design); the same key in clean/README.md is not flagged

candidate_tuned.config: fixtures/09-gitleaks/gitleaks-tuned.toml: extend default + rule for AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY assignments + allowlist for pk_test_/pk_live_

limits: Pattern rules need the real token format: during fixture building two fake keys with the wrong length (Google 36 instead of 35 chars, SendGrid 20 instead of 22) were missed or only caught by the generic rule. Real tokens have the right length; hand-typed fakes may not.
generic-api-key fires on publishable keys near the word 'key'; allowlist them in the config.
`dir` mode scans the working tree only; `git` mode is needed to catch secrets in history.
--redact replaces the secret in the report; the report still names file and line.
trials.reason: 10/10 fake secrets found in 0.1 s with 0 false positives on 10 look-alike files; single native binary, Windows build available, MIT.

install.command: claude plugin install mattpocock-skills@claude-plugins-official  (or copy SKILL.md into .claude/skills/diagnosing-bugs/)

trials.fixtures: fixtures/10-skill: 3 small Node modules with one seeded bug each and a README bug report (t1 off-by-one in a date range, t2 async race in a price feed, t3 unit-conversion constants), hidden tests (20 total: 7 + 5 + 8) in hidden-tests/, grade.mjs. Hidden tests fail 6/5/4 on the buggy code and pass 20/20 on reference fixes.
trials.design: Arm A = plain subagent with the bug report. Arm B = identical prompt preceded by the full SKILL.md and 'follow this skill exactly'. 2 reps per arm per task = 12 runs, launched concurrently, each in a fresh copy of the task folder. Graded only by scripts (grade.mjs runs the hidden tests after the run). Tokens, tool calls and wall time come from the harness usage report of each subagent (runs/10-skill/usage.jsonl); the token figure includes each subagent's fixed context, so compare the difference, not the absolute.

candidate_tuned.config: none: a second config (e.g. the skill as a /slash command instead of inline) was not run; the inline form is the one the Owner would use in a subagent

observations: Both arms fixed all three bugs in every rep; the hidden tests cannot separate them.

Arm B visibly followed the skill: red test before the fix in 6/6 runs, falsified alternative hypotheses named in the reply, one run added a 1000-iteration stress loop for the race. Arm A wrote tests after the fix in 6/6 runs and still passed.
The skill text is ~2.4 K tokens per run and the extra phases cost ~1.7 more tool calls and ~27 s per bug; on this task size that is pure overhead.
Bugs were small and well described (a README with exact numbers). The skill targets hard, badly described bugs; this trial does not measure that case.
limits: n = 2 reps per cell; the effect on tokens/time is consistent across all 3 tasks but the sample is small.
Tasks are synthetic and easy for a plain agent (ceiling effect: 40/40 in arm A). A harder task set (hidden, multi-file, flaky) is needed to see any quality gain.
Token counts include the subagent's fixed system context, so only the A-B difference is meaningful.
Runs were concurrent (12 at once); wall time has shared-CPU noise, the direction (B ~2x) is far outside it.
trials.verdict: REJECT (for small, well-described bugs); WATCH for hard bugs, untested
trials.reason: No measurable quality gain (40/40 vs 40/40 hidden tests) at +10 % tokens, +39 % tool calls and +96 % wall time. Our rule is 'measured gain over the baseline': there is none here. Re-test only on a set of hard, poorly specified bugs where the plain agent actually fails.
